definition: To cut words or scenes thought to be offensive from a book or play, often weakening it.
example: Early collectors tended to bowdlerize old folk ballads, quietly dropping every crude verse.
nuance: Censor can mean banning a work outright, but bowdlerize means trimming its content, and the word usually signals disapproval of the cuts.
prompt: A publisher prepares a children's edition of a classic novel full of coarse language.
options: The publisher decided to bowdlerize the novel, swapping each curse for a mild word.
The publisher chose to bowdlerize the novel by adding even saltier insults to the dialogue.
The publisher wanted to bowdlerize the novel by printing it in a larger, rounder font.
Critics expect to bowdlerize the novel with glowing reviews in every newspaper.
reasons: Replacing offensive language with tamer words is exactly this kind of prudish editing.
Adding coarse material is the reverse of stripping it out.
Changing the typeface alters the look of the page, not its objectionable content.
Praising a book has nothing to do with cutting passages from it.

practice.prompt: A theater company stages a centuries-old comedy for a family audience.
options: To bowdlerize the comedy, the director cut its rude puns and softened two songs.
The director chose to bowdlerize the comedy by restoring every rude line earlier versions had dropped.
The actors will bowdlerize the comedy by rehearsing it every evening for a month.
Audiences tend to bowdlerize the comedy, laughing loudest at its crudest scenes.
reasons: Removing and toning down improper material for propriety's sake fits the word.
Putting cut material back undoes expurgation rather than performing it.
Rehearsing is practice; it removes nothing offensive from the script.
Enjoying crude scenes is not editing them out; the word describes altering a text.
